label: Blue Note
rationale: Hill's second Blue Note session as leader and his most radical small-group experiment: a hornless quartet built on two simultaneous double basses — Richard Davis and Eddie Khan — with Roy Haynes, recorded December 13, 1963 at Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs, and held three years before release in August 1966 (BST 84160) [S1,S2,S3] (obs). Wikipedia and All About Jazz both single out the piano/two-bass/drums format as an instrumentation 'likely too unorthodox, even for a label that wasn't particularly averse to the unconventional' — the record is a defining document of Hill's method of writing for overlapping voices rather than a soloist-plus-rhythm [S1,S4] (obs). Lineage/session gravity: it shares its rhythm team with Black Fire (Richard Davis, Roy Haynes, November 1963) and sits directly in the run of Hill dates that culminates in Point of Departure, making it a load-bearing link in the Andrew Hill arc the canon already holds [S1,S3,S4] (inf). Dedications give the date a personal documentary value — 'Ode to Von' to saxophonist Von Freeman, 'Verne' to Hill's first wife Laverne Gillette — and '30 Pier Avenue' names The Lighthouse in Hermosa Beach [S1] (obs). It still plays: brooding, harmonically dense and unhurried, the record is the most atmospheric of Hill's Blue Note sessions [S4] (inf). Consensus is honest but moderate: Wikipedia's review box records AllMusic 3/5, DownBeat 3/5 and The Penguin Guide to Jazz 3/5 [S1] (obs) — the case here is Hill's arc and the unorthodox writing, not a canon-list sweep.

personnel_record.notes: Single session: December 13, 1963, Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs, NJ [S1,S2,S3]. Producer Alfred Lion and engineer Rudy Van Gelder are confirmed by the Apple Music credits [S8] and are the standard Blue Note house credits for a 1963 Van Gelder date [S1] (obs). Recorded 1963, released early August 1966 as Blue Note BST 84160; the year field is the 1963 recording year. Personnel is the quartet — Hill, two basses (Richard Davis and Eddie Khan), Roy Haynes — with no horns [S1,S2,S3,S4]. The one open conflict is Eddie Khan's coverage: prose sources say both basses play throughout, jazzdisco.org lists him on six of seven issued tracks; recorded, not resolved. The RVG and later CD editions add four alternate takes (of 'Smoke Stack', 'The Day After', 'Ode to Von' and 'Not So'); these are reissue-only and excluded above. Durations are the original LP timings. Sides are left null because no consulted source assigns the seven pieces to LP faces. track_assignments_complete is false — no source distinguishes per-track personnel beyond the quartet itself.

scope_check.boundary_note: Recorded in 1963 and squarely within the year window. Its post-bop foundation is in scope; the avant-garde edge raises a mild style-boundary question, but it is not a free-jazz gate case.

ballot.case_for: The hornless quartet of Hill, Richard Davis, Eddie Khan, and Roy Haynes makes this a striking experiment in writing for overlapping voices rather than a conventional soloist-plus-rhythm section (S1, S3, S4). Its place between Black Fire and Point of Departure gives it real lineage and session-gravity value within Hill’s 1963–65 Blue Note run, while All About Jazz describes an atmospheric, harmonically dense record with distinctive compositional character (S1, S4).
ballot.case_against: The dossier’s consensus evidence is modest: AllMusic, DownBeat, and the Penguin Guide each rate it 3/5, and it cites no major canon-list or anthology recognition (S1). The unusual two-bass format and brooding, dense sound may make it a rewarding Hill-arc supplement rather than a strong discovery gateway; its marginal case is less compelling beside the better-established Black Fire and Point of Departure.
ballot.disagreement: Both references judge the album contested, but differ on priority: Reference 1 says strong, emphasizing Hill’s arc and the defining format; Reference 2 says consider, emphasizing modest consensus and its satellite status. They also differ on scope: Reference 1 flags a mild avant-adjacent boundary, while Reference 2 sees no boundary in question.
ballot.recommendation: John should consider it as a distinctive Hill-arc supplement, weighing its unusual compositional method against its moderate consensus and less accessible sound.
